title: Epictetus goes free
hookLine: freed, he teaches in Rome, is banished with all philosophers by Domitian, and opens a school at Nicopolis around 93 CE

lines: A LAME MAN TEACHING IN ROME.
cards: Picture it: a lame, formerly enslaved man is teaching the sons of the powerful in Rome how to live. Then the emperor Domitian decides philosophers are a nuisance, and throws them all out of the city.
So where does a lame teacher with no city go now?

teach.b: At some point, and we don't know exactly when or how, Epictetus was set free. He'd already been studying philosophy while enslaved, with a Roman Stoic teacher named Musonius Rufus. Now he taught it himself.
Then came the exile; historians still debate the exact year. He lost his city, his students, whatever he'd built.
So he went across the sea to Nicopolis, a town on the western coast of Greece, and opened a school. And people came.
Young men traveled, some of them a long way, to sit on hard benches and be questioned by this lame teacher. As far as we know, he never wrote a book.

We have his teaching only because one student, Arrian, wrote down what he said, and later published it as the Discourses and a short handbook. Through them, you can hear him in class. He imagines a tyrant threatening him.
You'll chain me? You can chain my leg. But my will, not even Zeus himself can take that.
A thief once stole the iron lamp from his little shrine at home. His response: next time I'll buy a clay one.
Then the twist: the thief lost more than I did. He paid for a lamp by becoming a thief.

The Greek word he kept coming back to was prohairesis, usually translated will, or choice: your power to decide how you'll meet what happens. Owned, lamed, freed, exiled: everything outside kept being taken.
The school at Nicopolis was real, with benches and walls.
But the school he actually taught was one you carry inside, and no emperor can banish it.

how: Modern Stoics often keep a short written list of what is truly in their power, their own choices and responses, and read the Discourses and Handbook of Epictetus as a daily guide.

o: the power of reason that sets humans apart from animals
a calm acceptance of whatever fate sends your way
your power to choose how you'll meet what happens

games.q: from Rome to Nicopolis — tap the pairs.
p: his school on Greece's west coast
the student who wrote it down

s: he never wrote a book. his student Arrian wrote down what he said.
after his lamp was stolen, Epictetus said the thief lost more
he paid for a lamp by becoming a thief.
he opened a school at Nicopolis, and students came to him there.

games.q: you're Epictetus, and a thief has stolen the iron lamp from your home. what do you do?
o: buy a cheaper clay lamp, and decide the thief lost more.
games.why: a clay lamp next time. and the thief? he paid for a lamp by becoming a thief.

practice: Sit, and let the breath settle, then ask: what's one thing no one can take from me? Not an object, something inside: the way you treat people, your sense of humor, a memory, what you choose to pay attention to.
Let an answer come, and rest with it.

wordCard.voice: Prohairesis. Will, or choice: the part of you that decides how to meet what happens, and the one thing Epictetus never lost.

orig.note: Greek, prohairesis: will, choice, the power to decide how you meet what happens. Epictetus's central word.

carryVoice: Your line: the school is inside. Benches and walls can be taken; that one can't. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 15.11 (Domitian's expulsion of the philosophers)
